sections.title: Backlog & Segment Mix

charts.title: Revenue by Business Group
charts.annotation: Six reporting lines roll up into two segments elsewhere in this dashboard: Intelligent Devices (hardware, Sensors + Final Control) and Software & Systems (AspenTech, DeltaV/Ovation, Test & Measurement/NI).

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Emerson Electric Co.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

backlog.title: Order backlog
backlog.content:
Backlog is the dollar value of orders received but not yet shipped or recognized as revenue -- a forward-looking demand signal that complements trailing revenue.

For Emerson Electric Co.: management points to a multi-year, project-driven backlog (~$8.6bn at FY2025) as support for Final Control and engineered-systems revenue visibility; the business-group split (Intelligent Devices, Software & Systems, Safety & Productivity) is a new FY2025 disclosure, so only one year has the full breakdown.

What to watch:

  • Backlog growing faster than revenue (orders outpacing conversion, a leading indicator)
  • Backlog shrinking while revenue holds up (working down a book, not a demand signal yet)
  • Which business group is driving the change once more years of disclosure accumulate

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by business group
segmentRevenue.content:
Emerson discloses revenue across six finer business groups within its two reporting segments: Intelligent Devices is hardware (Sensors & Final Control, tied to industrial capex cycles); Software & Systems is AspenTech, DeltaV/Ovation (Control Systems & Software) and National Instruments (Test & Measurement), with more recurring/renewal revenue.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the investment case rests on Software & Systems growing faster and smoothing out the hardware groups' capex cyclicality -- this chart is the direct check on that mix shift.

What to watch:

  • Software & Systems (AspenTech, Test & Measurement, Control Systems & Software) share of total rising over time
  • Intelligent Devices hardware groups (Sensors, Final Control) tracking the industrial capex cycle
  • Only FY2024-FY2025 carry the full six-way split so far

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Emerson Electric Co.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Emerson Electric Co.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Emerson Electric Co.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
